主要内容: In 2019, the retail industry faced a wave of bankruptcies, with companies like Forever 21, Barneys New York, Sugarfina, and Destination Maternity filing for bankruptcy. Some retailers, such as Z Gallerie and Charming Charlie, returned to bankruptcy court for the second time, while others, like Fred's, liquidated their businesses entirely. Vince Tibone, a retail analyst, noted that 2019 was another significant year for retail bankruptcies, following 2017 and 2018. The apparel category was particularly affected, with numerous clothing retailers like Charlotte Russe, Diesel, A'Gaci, and Forever 21 filing for bankruptcy. This trend followed the department store bankruptcies of Sears and Bon-Ton in 2018. The shift in consumer behavior, with shoppers turning to platforms like Rent the Runway and Stitch Fix, or to stores like Target and TJ Maxx, contributed to the decline of traditional department stores. According to CB Insights, there were 23 retail bankruptcies in 2019, compared to 17 in 2018, with a total of 81 retail bankruptcies tracked since 2015. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several major retailers filed for bankruptcy. Shopko, a discount retail business, filed for bankruptcy in January, initially hoping to salvage some of its locations but ultimately liquidating all of its assets, including over 300 stores. Gymboree, which filed for bankruptcy for the second time in January, announced plans to shutter all 800 of its stores but later found buyers for its brands. Things Remembered, a popular gifting chain, filed for bankruptcy in February and was sold to Enesco, which planned to save fewer than half of its 450 stores. Payless Shoesource, which filed for bankruptcy for the second time in February, announced the closure of over 2,000 stores across North America. Charlotte Russe, a teen apparel retailer, also filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February, signaling the ongoing struggles of the retail sector during this period. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several well-known brands filed for bankruptcy. Forever 21, a popular fast-fashion brand, was among those affected, with its brand and intellectual property sold to North American fashion house YM. YM planned to keep dozens of Charlotte Russe locations open. Diesel, another brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March, citing sinking sales and expensive real estate deals as reasons for its financial struggles. Z Gallerie, a home furnishings retailer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy for the second time, attributing its struggles to being late to invest in e-commerce. Roberto Cavalli, a luxury fashion brand, filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in April, liquidating its entire North American business after losing its chief creative director. Charming Charlie, a youthful apparel brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July, marking its second filing, and later sold its intellectual property to CJS Group. A'Gaci, a women's fashion brand, also filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August, marking its second time in bankruptcy court in under two years. In 2019, several major retailers faced bankruptcy, including Avenue, Barneys New York, Fred's, and Forever 21. Avenue, a plus-size apparel brand, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August and later transitioned to Chapter 7, beginning the liquidation of over 200 stores. Barneys New York, a high-end department store chain, also filed for Chapter 11 in August, with its brands and intellectual property sold to Authentic Brands. Fred's, a discount retailer and pharmacy chain, filed for Chapter 11 in September, planning to liquidate over 500 stores. Forever 21, an apparel retailer, filed for Chapter 11 in September, with over 800 stores worldwide, and planned to exit most international markets. These bankruptcies highlighted challenges in the retail industry, including competition from larger rivals and operational difficulties. In 2019, the retail industry faced significant challenges as several companies filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. One notable case was Sugarfina, a luxury candy brand known for its unique gummy bear and chocolate flavors. Sugarfina filed for bankruptcy in September 2019, listing assets and liabilities of up to $50 million. Private-equity firm Bristol Luxury Group acquired its assets in November, vowing to keep some stores open. Sugarfina also operated smaller shops in some Nordstrom locations. Another major player was Destination Maternity, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2019. The company, which owned maternity brands like A Pea in the Pod and Motherhood Maternity, had over 400 stores at the time. Marquee Brands acquired its assets in early December, stating it was evaluating all aspects of the business, including its retail store network. The future of Destination Maternity's locations under new ownership remains uncertain. These bankruptcies highlight the struggles faced by the retail sector during this period.
